questions.q: Which are the four pillars of object-oriented programming?
o: Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism
Compilation, linking, loading and execution
Class, object, method and variable
Public, private, protected and static
questions.w: Most interviews expect a short definition plus a quick example for each of the four.

questions.q: What does encapsulation mean in practice?
o: Keep state private and expose behaviour through an interface
Make every field public for easy access
Put every class together in a single file
Copy objects instead of ever sharing them
questions.w: Callers cannot put the object in an invalid state, and the internals can change without breaking them.

o: One call behaves differently depending on the actual object type
A class that has been declared with a great many fields
Methods that are able to return several values at once
A class that gets compiled several times in a build
questions.w: Runtime (overriding) polymorphism lets code depend on an interface such as `PaymentMethod` while each implementation behaves its own way.

questions.q: What is the difference between overloading and overriding?
o: Overloading: same name, new parameters. Overriding: a subclass replaces a method
Overloading is decided at run time, overriding at compile time
Overloading means changing only the return type of a method
They are simply two different names for the same mechanism
questions.w: Overloads are chosen at compile time from the argument types. Overrides are chosen at run time from the object's real class.

questions.q: When should you prefer composition over inheritance?
o: You reuse behaviour without a rigid is-a hierarchy
Only when the class has no methods at all
Whenever a class needs to hold fields
Never, because inheritance is always better
questions.w: Inheritance couples subclass to superclass internals. Composition allows swapping parts at runtime and is easier to test.

questions.q: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in Java?
o: A class can implement many interfaces but extend one abstract class that may hold state
Interfaces can hold instance fields, while abstract classes cannot hold any
Abstract classes are not allowed to contain implemented methods
Interfaces can be instantiated directly with the `new` keyword
questions.w: Since Java 8 interfaces can have default methods, but still no instance state. Use an abstract class to share state and code.

questions.q: A `Square` extends `Rectangle` but breaks code that sets width and height separately. Which principle is violated?
o: Liskov substitution: a subtype must work wherever its base type does
Open-closed: classes should be closed to extension
Single responsibility: one reason to change
Interface segregation: keep interfaces small
questions.w: If substituting the subtype changes expected behaviour, the inheritance hierarchy is wrong.

o: Exposing what an object does while hiding how it does it
Splitting a single class across many different source files
Declaring every method of a class as static for speed
Removing code from the project once it is no longer used
questions.w: Callers use `Repository.save(x)` without knowing whether it writes to SQL, a file or memory.
